title: Chapter XXXII
paragraphs: 1802.—This September a friend in the north invited me to help devastate the game on his moors. On my way to his house, I unexpectedly found myself within fifteen miles of Gimmerton. At a roadside inn, the stableman was holding a bucket of water for my horses when a cart passed laden with newly cut oats, still very green. “That’s from Gimmerton, that is!” he remarked. “They’re allus three weeks behind other folk wi’ their harvest.”
“Gimmerton?” I repeated. My time in that neighbourhood already seemed dim and dreamlike. “Ah! Yes. How far is it from here?”
“Maybe fourteen miles over t’ hills,” he answered. “And a rough road.”

I suddenly felt an urge to visit Thrushcross Grange. It was barely noon, and I thought I might as well sleep under my own roof as at an inn. Besides, I could easily spare a day to settle matters with my landlord and save myself another journey into the neighbourhood. After resting a while, I told my servant to ask the way to the village. We covered the distance in about three hours, greatly tiring our horses.

I left him there and went on alone down the valley. The grey church looked greyer, the lonely churchyard lonelier. I saw a moorland sheep cropping the short grass on the graves. The weather was lovely and warm—too warm for travelling—but the heat did not spoil my pleasure in the beautiful scenery above and below. Had I seen it nearer August, I am sure it would have tempted me to idle away a month in those solitary places. Nothing could be drearier in winter, or more heavenly in summer, than those valleys enclosed by hills and those bold, steep swells of heather.

I reached the Grange before sunset and knocked. But a single thin curl of blue smoke rising from the kitchen chimney suggested that the household had withdrawn to the back, and no one heard me. I rode into the yard. A girl of nine or ten sat knitting under the porch, while an old woman reclined on the steps, thoughtfully smoking a pipe.
“Is Mrs. Dean in?” I asked the old woman.
“Mistress Dean? Nay!” she answered. “She doesn’t live here. She’s up at t’ Heights.”
“Then are you the housekeeper?” I asked.
“Aye, I keep t’ house,” she replied.
“Well, I’m Mr. Lockwood, the master. I wonder whether there’s a room for me? I’d like to stay the night.”
“T’ master!” she cried in amazement. “Why, who knew ye were coming? Ye should have sent word. There’s nowt dry or decent about t’ place—not a thing!”

She dropped her pipe and hurried inside, followed by the girl and then me. I soon saw that her description was accurate and that my unwelcome appearance had almost driven her out of her wits. I told her to calm herself. I would go for a walk; meanwhile she should try to prepare a corner of a sitting room for my supper and a bedroom for the night. There was no need to sweep or dust: a good fire and dry sheets would be enough. She seemed eager to do her best, though she thrust the hearth brush into the grate instead of the poker and put several other tools to equally unsuitable uses. I left, trusting her energy to provide somewhere to rest on my return. Wuthering Heights was my destination. Just after leaving the yard, another thought brought me back.
“Is everyone well at the Heights?” I asked her.
“Aye, for all I know!” she answered, hurrying away with a pan of hot cinders.

I wanted to ask why Mrs. Dean had left the Grange, but at such a crisis I could not detain the woman, so I turned and went. I walked at leisure, with the glow of the setting sun behind me and the gentle splendour of the rising moon ahead, one fading as the other brightened. Leaving the park, I climbed the stony side road to Mr. Heathcliff’s house. Before it came into sight, all that remained of daylight was a flat amber glow in the west. Yet the magnificent moon showed every pebble in the path and every blade of grass. I had neither to climb the gate nor knock: it opened at my touch. An improvement, I thought. My nose discovered another: the fragrance of stocks and wallflowers drifted through the air from among the familiar fruit trees.

The doors and windows were open, yet a fine red fire lit the hearth, as is usual in a coal district. The comfort of the sight makes the extra heat bearable. Besides, the main room at Wuthering Heights is large enough for its occupants to sit well beyond the fire’s warmth. Those present had accordingly settled near a window. Before entering I could see them and hear their conversation, and so I watched and listened, drawn by a mixture of curiosity and envy that grew the longer I lingered.
“Con-_trary_!” said a voice sweet as a silver bell. “That’s the third time, you dunce! I won’t tell you again. Remember, or I’ll pull your hair!”
“Contrary, then,” another voice answered, deep but gentle. “Now kiss me for getting it right.”
“No. Read it through correctly first, without one mistake.”

The young man began reading. He was respectably dressed and seated at a table with a book before him. His handsome face glowed with pleasure, and his eyes kept straying impatiently from the page to a small white hand over his shoulder. Whenever its owner caught these signs of inattention, a brisk slap on his cheek brought him back to his work. She stood behind him, her bright, fair ringlets sometimes mingling with his brown hair as she bent over to guide his studies. Her face—it was fortunate he could not see her face, or he would never have stayed so attentive. I could see it, and bit my lip with resentment at having thrown away whatever chance I might once have had to do more than stare at its devastating beauty.

The lesson ended, though not without further mistakes. The pupil claimed his reward and received at least five kisses, which he generously returned. Then they came to the door. From their conversation I gathered that they meant to walk on the moors. I supposed Hareton Earnshaw would condemn me, inwardly if not aloud, to the deepest pit of hell if I showed my unfortunate face near him just then. Feeling thoroughly small and spiteful, I slunk round to seek refuge in the kitchen. That entrance was open too. By the door sat my old friend Nelly Dean, sewing and singing, though her song was repeatedly interrupted from inside by harsh expressions of contempt and intolerance delivered in a far from musical voice.

“I’d far rather have them swearing in my ears from morning till night than listen to ye at all!” said the occupant of the kitchen, answering something I had not heard Nelly say. “It’s a blazing shame I can’t open t’ blessed Book without ye starting up those praises of Satan and all t’ dreadful wickedness ever born into this world! Oh! Ye’re a right good-for-nowt, and so is she, and that poor lad’ll be lost between ye. Poor lad!” he added with a groan. “He’s bewitched, I’m certain of it. Oh, Lord, judge them, for there’s neither law nor justice among our rulers!”

“No! Or I suppose we’d be sitting in burning bundles of sticks,” the singer retorted. “But hush, old man. Read your Bible like a Christian and leave me alone. This is ‘Fairy Annie’s Wedding,’ a lovely tune, and you can dance to it.”

Mrs. Dean was about to begin again when I stepped forward. Recognising me at once, she sprang up. “Why, bless you, Mr. Lockwood! How could you think of coming back like this? Thrushcross Grange is all shut up. You should have let us know!”
“I’ve arranged to stay there for as long as I need,” I replied. “I leave again tomorrow. But how did you come to be transplanted here, Mrs. Dean? Tell me that.”
“Zillah left, and soon after you went to London Mr. Heathcliff asked me to come and stay until you returned. But do come in! Have you walked from Gimmerton this evening?”
“From the Grange,” I answered. “While they make a room ready for me, I want to finish my business with your master. I don’t expect another opportunity soon.”
“What business, sir?” Nelly asked, leading me inside. “He’s out at the moment and won’t be back for a while.”
“The rent,” I answered.
“Oh! Then you’ll have to settle that with Mrs. Heathcliff,” she said, “or rather with me. She hasn’t learnt to manage her affairs yet, so I act for her. There’s no one else.”
I looked surprised.
“Ah! I see you haven’t heard of Heathcliff’s death,” she continued.
“Heathcliff dead!” I exclaimed in astonishment. “How long ago?”
“Three months. But sit down and give me your hat, and I’ll tell you everything. Wait—you haven’t had anything to eat, have you?”
“I don’t need anything. I’ve ordered supper at home. Sit down yourself. I never imagined he’d die! Tell me how it happened. You say they won’t be back for some time—the young people?”
“No. I have to scold them every evening for walking out so late, but they take no notice of me. At least have some of our old ale. It’ll do you good; you look tired.”

She hurried to fetch it before I could refuse. I heard Joseph asking whether “it wasn’t a crying scandal for her to have men following her at her age? And then to fetch those jugs out of t’ master’s cellar! He was fair ashamed to stand by and watch it.”

She did not pause to answer him, but returned a moment later with a silver pint mug foaming at the brim. I praised its contents with appropriate enthusiasm. Then she told me the rest of Heathcliff’s story. He had come to a “queer” end, as she put it.

Within a fortnight of your departure, she said, I was summoned to Wuthering Heights, and for Catherine’s sake I went gladly. My first meeting with her shocked and grieved me: she had changed so much since we parted. Mr. Heathcliff gave no reason for changing his mind about my coming. He merely said he wanted me and was tired of seeing Catherine. I was to use the little parlour as my sitting room and keep her with me. Having to see her once or twice a day was enough for him. She seemed pleased with this arrangement. Gradually I smuggled over a great many books and other things that had amused her at the Grange, and persuaded myself we would be reasonably comfortable. That illusion did not last. Catherine was content at first, but soon became irritable and restless. For one thing, she was forbidden to go beyond the garden, and as spring approached its narrow limits distressed her terribly. For another, my household duties often forced me to leave her, and she complained of loneliness. She preferred quarrelling with Joseph in the kitchen to sitting peacefully alone. I did not mind their skirmishes. But when the master wanted the main room to himself, Hareton too was often driven into the kitchen. At first she either left when he came or quietly helped with my work, avoiding any mention of him or word to him; and he remained as sullen and silent as he could. After a while, though, she changed. She could no longer leave him alone. She spoke at him, commented on his stupidity and laziness, and wondered aloud how he could bear his life—how he could spend a whole evening staring at the fire and dozing.

“He’s just like a dog, isn’t he, Ellen?” she said once. “Or a cart horse? He works, eats, and sleeps for ever! What an empty, dreary mind he must have! Do you ever dream, Hareton? If you do, what about? But you can’t speak to me!”
She looked at him, but he would neither answer nor look back.
“Perhaps he’s dreaming now,” she went on. “His shoulder twitched just like Juno’s. Ask him, Ellen.”
“If you don’t behave, Mr. Hareton will ask the master to send you upstairs!” I said. He had not merely twitched his shoulder; he had clenched his fist, as though tempted to use it.

“I know why Hareton never speaks when I’m in the kitchen,” she exclaimed another time. “He’s afraid I’ll laugh at him. Ellen, what do you think? He once started teaching himself to read, and because I laughed he burnt his books and gave it up. Wasn’t that foolish?”
“And weren’t you unkind?” I said. “Answer that.”
“Perhaps I was,” she continued, “but I didn’t expect him to be so silly. Hareton, if I gave you a book now, would you take it? I’ll try!”
She laid the book she had been reading on his hand. He flung it away and muttered that if she did not stop he would break her neck.
“Well, I’ll put it here,” she said, “in the table drawer. I’m going to bed.”

She whispered that I should watch whether he touched it, then left. But he would not go near it. When I told her the next morning, she was bitterly disappointed. I could see she regretted his continuing sullenness and idleness. Her conscience reproached her for driving him away from self-improvement; she had done that thoroughly. But her ingenuity was now working to repair the harm. While I ironed or did other work that kept me in one place and could not easily be done in the parlour, she would bring an entertaining book and read aloud. If Hareton was there, she generally stopped at an interesting point and left the book lying about. She tried this repeatedly, but he was stubborn as a mule. Instead of taking the bait, in wet weather he began smoking with Joseph. They sat like two mechanical figures on opposite sides of the fire, the older man fortunately too deaf to understand her wicked nonsense, as he would have called it, and the younger doing his best to appear indifferent. On fine evenings Hareton went shooting. Catherine yawned and sighed, pestered me to talk to her, then ran into the yard or garden the moment I began. Finally she resorted to tears, saying she was tired of living and that her life was useless.

Mr. Heathcliff, increasingly averse to company, had almost entirely banished Earnshaw from his room. An accident early in March confined Hareton to the kitchen for several days. His gun burst while he was alone on the hills. A splinter cut his arm, and he lost a great deal of blood before he reached home. He was consequently forced to rest beside the fire until he recovered. Catherine liked having him there. At any rate, she hated her upstairs room more than ever and made me find jobs downstairs so she could come with me.

On Easter Monday Joseph took some cattle to Gimmerton fair. That afternoon I was busy ironing linen in the kitchen. Earnshaw sat in the chimney corner, as gloomy as ever. My little mistress passed an idle hour drawing pictures on the windowpanes, varying her amusement with subdued snatches of song, whispered exclamations, and quick, irritated, impatient glances towards her cousin. He steadily smoked and stared into the grate. When I told her I could do without her blocking my light any longer, she moved to the hearth. I paid little attention to what she was doing, but soon heard her begin: “Hareton, I’ve realised that I want—that I’m glad—that I’d like you to be my cousin now, if you hadn’t become so cross with me and so rough.”
Hareton gave no answer.
“Hareton, Hareton, Hareton! Can you hear me?” she continued.
“Get away with ye!” he growled, utterly unyielding.
“Let me have that pipe,” she said, cautiously reaching out and taking it from his mouth.
Before he could try to recover it, she had broken it and thrown it behind the fire. He swore at her and grabbed another.
“Wait!” she cried. “You must listen first. I can’t talk with those clouds floating in my face.”
“Will ye go to the devil!” he snarled, “and leave me alone!”

“No, I won’t,” she persisted. “I don’t know how to make you talk to me, and you’re determined not to understand. When I call you stupid, I don’t mean anything. I don’t mean I despise you. Come, Hareton, you must take notice of me. You’re my cousin, and you must acknowledge me.”

“I’ll have nowt to do with thee, thy filthy pride, or thy damned mocking tricks!” he answered. “I’ll go to hell, body and soul, before I so much as look thy way again. Get out of t’ way, now, this minute!”
Catherine frowned and went back to the window seat, biting her lip and trying to hide her growing urge to sob by humming an odd tune.
“You ought to make friends with your cousin, Mr. Hareton,” I put in, “since she’s sorry for her rudeness. It would do you a world of good. Having her for company would make a different man of you.”
“Company!” he cried. “When she hates me and doesn’t think me fit to wipe her shoes! Nay, even if it made me a king, I won’t be scorned again for trying to please her.”
“I’m not the one who hates you—you hate me!” Cathy wept, no longer hiding her distress. “You hate me as much as Mr. Heathcliff does, and more.”

“You’re a damned liar,” Earnshaw began. “Then why have I angered him a hundred times by taking your side? Even when you sneered at me and despised me, and—Keep plaguing me, and I’ll go in there and tell him you worried me out of the kitchen!”
“I didn’t know you’d taken my side,” she answered, drying her eyes. “I was miserable and bitter towards everyone. But now I thank you and ask you to forgive me. What more can I do?”

She came back to the hearth and openly held out her hand. He scowled darkly as a thundercloud, keeping his fists tightly closed and his eyes on the floor. Catherine must instinctively have understood that stubborn perversity, rather than dislike, lay behind his behaviour. After hesitating a moment, she bent and gently kissed his cheek. The little rogue thought I had not seen. She drew back and returned quite demurely to the window. I shook my head at her in reproach. She blushed and whispered, “Well! What else could I do, Ellen? He wouldn’t shake hands or look at me. I had to show him somehow that I like him and want to be friends.”
I cannot say whether the kiss persuaded Hareton. For several minutes he took great care to hide his face, and when he finally raised it, he seemed desperately uncertain where to look.
Catherine neatly wrapped a handsome book in white paper, tied it with a ribbon, and addressed it to “Mr. Hareton Earnshaw.” Then she asked me to act as her ambassadress and deliver the present.
“Tell him that if he’ll accept it, I’ll come and teach him to read it properly,” she said. “If he refuses, I’ll go upstairs and never bother him again.”

I carried it over and repeated the message, anxiously watched by the person who had sent me. Hareton would not unclench his fingers, so I put it on his knee. He did not knock it off. I went back to my work. Catherine rested her head and arms on the table until she heard the faint rustle of the paper being removed. Then she slipped away and quietly sat beside her cousin. He trembled and blushed. All his rudeness and sullen harshness had left him. At first he could not find the courage to answer her questioning look or whispered plea.
“Say you forgive me, Hareton. Please. That one little word would make me so happy.”
He muttered something I could not hear.
“And will you be my friend?” Catherine asked.
“Nay, thou’ll be ashamed of me every day of thy life,” he answered, “and the better thou knows me, the more ashamed thou’ll be. I can’t bear it.”
“So you won’t be my friend?” she said, smiling sweetly and edging closer.

I could make out no more of their conversation. But when I looked round again, two such radiant faces were bent over the accepted book that I had no doubt both sides had agreed to peace. From that moment, the enemies were sworn allies.

The book was full of expensive illustrations. These, and their situation, charmed them enough to keep them in their seats until Joseph returned. The poor man was appalled to see Catherine sitting on the same bench as Hareton Earnshaw, with her hand on his shoulder, and bewildered that his favourite tolerated her closeness. He was too deeply affected to comment that night. His feelings showed only in the immense sighs he gave as he solemnly opened his large Bible on the table and covered it with dirty banknotes from his pocketbook, the proceeds of the day’s business. Finally he called Hareton away.
“Take these in to t’ master, lad,” he said, “and stay there. I’m going up to my own room. This hole’s neither decent nor fit for us. We must clear out and find another.”
“Come, Catherine,” I said, “we must ‘clear out’ too. I’ve finished ironing. Are you ready?”
“It isn’t eight yet!” she answered, reluctantly getting up. “Hareton, I’ll leave this book on the mantelpiece and bring some more tomorrow.”
“Any books thou leaves here, I’ll take into t’ main room,” Joseph said, “and thou’ll be lucky to find them again. So please thysen!”

Cathy threatened that his library would pay for hers. Smiling at Hareton as she passed, she went upstairs singing, lighter-hearted, I venture to say, than she had ever been under that roof, except perhaps on her earliest visits to Linton.

The friendship that began this way grew quickly, though it suffered occasional interruptions. Earnshaw could not be made polished simply by wishing it, and my young mistress was no philosopher or model of patience. But their minds were moving towards the same end: one loved and wanted to respect, the other loved and wanted to be respected. In time they managed to reach it.

You see, Mr. Lockwood, winning Mrs. Heathcliff’s heart was easy enough. But now I’m glad you didn’t try. The marriage of those two will fulfil all my wishes. On their wedding day I shall envy nobody. There won’t be a happier woman in England!
